missing_in_a: explicit rejection of non-HTML Content-Type responses (B gates on text/html; weakly implied by 'web scraping')
response body size cap / memory bound (B: 10 MiB)
robots.txt compliance check (B gates on it; arguably part of polite scraping, not strictly implied)
missing_in_b: configurable extraction via CSS selector (A lets user choose what to scrape; B fixes title/text/links schema)
user-facing success feedback line on stdout (A's REQ-006; B's shown text has none)
CSV output option (A supports CSV and JSON; B is JSON-only — prompt didn't require both)
reasons: A gives a lean, fully traceable pipeline: every requirement has Given/When/Then acceptance criteria, and the spec pins the CLI, exact User-Agent, timeout, redirects, extraction, CSV/JSON output, and error handling — implementable as-is and consistent, matching the 'simple' request. B is heavily over-engineered versus 'simple' (robots gate, retries, 6 exit codes, size caps), its spec leaves the page-fetch User-Agent unstated, and both B documents are truncated mid-section (output module, error table, FR-005+), so an implementer must fill gaps.
